name: Gay-Lussacs's law
seoDesc: Gay-Lussacs's law: work out initial temperature (T₁) from the final pressure and the final temperature. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the final pressure, the final temperature, the volume and amount of gas and the Gay-Lussacs's law calculator solves for initial temperature (T₁). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Gay-Lussacs's law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Gay-Lussacs's law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports initial temperature (T₁) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the final pressure (p₂), the final temperature (T₂), the volume (V) and amount of gas (n).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Gay-Lussacs's law calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Initial temperature (T₁)=initial pressure (p₁) × final temperature (T₂) ÷ final pressure (p₂)
Initial temperature (T₁)=(5000000 ÷ 41572299) × initial pressure (p₁) × volume (V) ÷ amount of gas (n)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Initial pressure (p₁) = 10 Pa, Final pressure (p₂) = 10 Pa and Final temperature (T₂) = 10 K. The calculator returns Initial temperature (T₁) = 10 K.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Initial temperature (T₁) = 10 K should be roughly the size you expected from Initial pressure (p₁) = 10 Pa and Final pressure (p₂) = 10 Pa.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Mole, opening in moles

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Gay-Lussacs's law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the final pressure, the final temperature and the volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Gay-Lussacs's law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns initial temperature (T₁), derived from the final pressure, the final temperature and the volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Gay-Lussacs's law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the final pressure, the final temperature, the volume and amount of gas, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial pressure (p₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial pressure (p₁) opens in pascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Initial temperature (T₁) = 10 K. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Gay-Lussacs's law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
